summary: Literary criticism and reception from Indonesia, Bengal, Senegal and Guyana broaden the evidence beyond Anglo-American lists. Character-model speculation and film/book distinctions remain explicit.
next: Continue multilingual literary criticism and independent philosophical reviews.

sources.title: The Golden Muse
sources.note: Zoellner contrasts Harris’s difficult colonial allegory with Carew’s accessible mining novel, and praises Hart’s monetary explanation while criticizing abandoned narrative threads.
candidates: Gold: The Race for the World’s Most Seductive Metal
sources.limits: Comparative judgment is one critic’s; the author discloses friendship with another reviewed writer.

targets.L: Harris and Carew receive contrasting formal judgments.
targets.N: Hart’s explanatory strengths and narrative weaknesses.

sources.title: The power of Pramoedya
sources.note: Hollier follows Minke’s education through colonial contradictions and Nyai Ontosoroh’s teaching; the novels challenged the reviewer’s inherited Australian assumptions.
sources.limits: Personal reception and interpretation, not a comparative ranking.

sources.title: A lesson in courage
sources.note: Christanty recalls secretly reading the Buru novels under censorship, praising physical description, historical conviction and flawed, resistant characters who shaped her activism.
sources.limits: Retrospective personal testimony; quoted claims about Nobel eligibility are not endorsed.

targets.A: Documented effects of fiction on a writer.
targets.L: Specific narrative virtues and Indonesian reception.

sources.title: Truth/Untruth: Mahasweta Devi’s novel about a pregnant maid’s death is as comedic as it is morbid
sources.note: Debnath reads Devi’s unsentimental treatment of a maid’s death through caste impersonation, class ambition and gendered exploitation.
sources.location: Opening critical assessment and plot discussion
sources.limits: One translated novel; reviewer enthusiasm is not worldwide consensus.

targets.A: Bengali fiction absent from dominant lists.

sources.title: Stories untold
sources.note: Keïta investigates family testimony connecting a relative to Bagayoko, using migration and naming histories to explore the novel’s possible historical models.
sources.location: Opening family testimony and patronym discussion
sources.limits: The proposed character model is conjectural, not established authorship evidence.

targets.A: Historical research on a Senegalese novel.

sources.title: Ousmane Sembene invented a new cinema for Africa
sources.note: Gadjigo describes God’s Bits of Wood restoring connections to local places and people after alienating schooling, before explaining Sembène’s turn toward cinema.
sources.limits: Film achievements are not transferred to book merit.

targets.A: First-person account of a novel’s influence.

sources.title: Decolonizing African literature begins with language
sources.note: Criticizes a classroom canon that reduces African authors to one familiar book and channels recognition through metropolitan publishing and European languages.
sources.location: Language and fixed classroom canon discussion
sources.limits: English/French versions are one underlying essay; examples are not ranked.
